r.정치 구도: Pakistan is a federation of four provinces with a parliamentary system led by a prime minister. But the army has ruled directly for almost half the years since independence in 1947, and it has kept control of security and foreign policy under civilian governments too. No prime minister has ever completed a full term. In 2022 a prime minister who had fallen out with the army was removed in a no-confidence vote and jailed the following year. In the February 2024 election independents backed by his party won the most seats, but the two traditional parties joined forces to form the government. In November 2025 the constitution was amended so that the army chief also serves as Chief of Defence Forces, commanding all three services, and a new Federal Constitutional Court was placed above the Supreme Court for constitutional cases. Supreme Court judges resigned in protest, and critics say the change wrote the military's power into the constitution.

t.why: It is the only Muslim-majority state with nuclear weapons. It has fought India, also nuclear-armed, over Kashmir since independence, and in May 2025 the two traded missiles and drones for four days after tourists were killed in Kashmir. India then stopped honoring the 1960 treaty that divides the waters of the Indus. In August 2026 a Court of Arbitration ruled that the treaty remains in force, but India rejects the decision. For a country whose farms depend on the Indus, the dispute is about survival. China is tied in through an economic corridor of roads and power plants running to the port of Gwadar on the Arabian Sea, and in September 2025 Pakistan signed a defense pact with Saudi Arabia under which an attack on one is treated as an attack on both. Bordering Iran and close to the United States, it stepped in as mediator in the 2026 war. It brokered a ceasefire in April, hosted high-level US-Iran talks in Islamabad, and in June signed as mediator the memorandum the two sides agreed. With the Taliban government in Afghanistan it clashed over militants along the border, going as far as air strikes on Kabul in October 2025.
t.rel: Always tense with India over Kashmir. It is so close to China that the two call each other 'iron brothers', and it clashes often with Afghanistan over militants on the border.
t.korea: The two countries established diplomatic relations in 1983. Since the 1990s South Korea's Economic Development Cooperation Fund has financed roads, hospitals and a technology park in Pakistan. Because the country is short of electricity, Korean state companies have invested in hydropower in the northern mountains: K-water built and runs the Patrind plant and Korea South-East Power the Gulpur plant. Hyundai Motor and Kia assemble cars there with local partners.
t.know: It has five peaks above 8,000 m, including K2, the world's second highest.
etext: Cotton grown in the Indus basin becomes yarn, cloth and clothing, and textiles make up more than half of exports. Pakistani mills supply towels, bed linen, knitwear and jeans to global brands. Basmati rice is another big export. But the industry has stayed with raw cotton and cheap goods and has not grown exports the way Bangladesh or Vietnam did.

Money sent home by workers in the Gulf, Britain and the United States is larger than goods exports. In the 2025-26 fiscal year it passed $40 billion, a record. That money covers the large trade deficit.

Imports far exceed exports and few people pay tax, so dollars run out every few years. Pakistan has gone to the IMF more than 20 times and came close to default in 2023. Under a $7 billion program that began in 2024 it is cutting subsidies and widening the tax net.

Reko Diq in Balochistan holds one of the world's large copper and gold deposits and is being developed by Canada's Barrick. China built power plants, roads and the port of Gwadar under the economic corridor. That eased power shortages but left debt and fixed payments to the power plants as a burden.

Oil and gas are bought from the Gulf, so reserves drain quickly when prices rise. The country is exposed to climate disasters such as the great floods of 2022, and political instability and militant attacks in the border regions deter investors.
